name: Dry brush

lead: Dry brushing is stroking a stiff natural-bristle brush over dry skin, usually before a shower and in long strokes toward the heart. People use it for smoother, softer-looking body skin and a pink, awake-looking glow.

The bristles lift dead surface cells and briefly raise blood flow to the skin, which gives the smoother, pinker look. Dermatological experts generally support exfoliation and temporary smoothness as direct effects. Proponents also claim lymph drainage, detoxification, and reduced cellulite; the secondary sources reviewed found no rigorous trials for those claims, and clinical lymphatic drainage is a separate, trained technique.

paras: People brush dry skin for a few minutes before showering, starting at the feet and working upward, then rinse and moisturize. It is a low-cost routine often done several times a week, with smoothness showing right after.

It is generally considered safe on intact skin if gentle, but is advised against on rashes, eczema, psoriasis, sunburn, wounds, or active acne. Over-brushing damages the skin barrier, and brushes need regular cleaning.

angle.text: Users brush dry skin before showering to exfoliate dead cells and leave the surface smoother and pinker. Some also credit it with lymph drainage and a leaner look, though the sources reviewed found no rigorous trials for those claims.

lead: Dry brushing, also called dry skin brushing or garshana, is the practice of stroking a stiff, natural-bristle brush over dry skin, usually before a shower and in long strokes toward the heart. People use it to get smoother, softer, pinker-looking skin on the body, and some hope it also softens the look of cellulite.[1]

Cleveland Clinic dermatologist Shilpi Khetarpal describes dry brushing as excellent for exfoliating rough, dry skin, and says increased blood flow can make skin look temporarily plumper.[2] Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, links the practice to Ayurvedic garshana and to the Japanese dry-towel friction practice kanpu masatsu.[1]

Proponents also describe it as stimulating circulation, promoting lymphatic drainage and supporting detoxification. Dermatologists and review articles say these broader claims have not been tested in controlled trials, and that the confirmed effect is mechanical exfoliation of the skin surface.[2][3]

paras: The brush is typically long-handled with firm natural bristles such as boar hair or plant fibres like sisal, and is applied for a few minutes on completely dry skin, without oils or lotions.[1] Softer brushes are described for sensitive skin and firmer ones for resilient skin, and short palm-style brushes allow more precise control.[1] A session is usually followed by a shower and moisturiser.[1][2]

Grokipedia says the practice traces to Ayurvedic medicine, where it is called garshana, traditionally done with raw silk or linen gloves. It also describes the Japanese practice kanpu masatsu, popular in the 1940s, and says dry brushing spread in Western wellness culture in the late twentieth century through naturopathic and holistic movements.[1] These historical statements come from an AI-generated source and were not independently confirmed.

sections.h: Claimed effects and what experts say
paras: Proponents describe the bristles as abrading dead cells and briefly increasing blood flow, producing a smoother, pink look. The lymph-drainage claim rests on stroking toward the heart and major lymph nodes.[1] Khetarpal says dry brushing helps exfoliate and can promote circulation, but that not all claimed benefits hold up.[2]

On cellulite, Khetarpal says no scientific evidence shows that dry brushing reduces it, and that any visible improvement is likely a temporary plumping of the skin from increased blood flow.[2] A News-Medical overview states that most claims originate in magazine and spa marketing, that skin-rubbing studies found only brief changes in temperature and pulse, and that no clinical data show meaningfully faster lymph clearance. It describes dry brushing as the most superficial exfoliation method, with stronger documented effects reported for chemical exfoliants and microdermabrasion.[3] The overview also notes that a related Japanese dry-towel study (Komagata, 2023) addressed a different technique.[3]
No studies found that test dry brushing on skin appearance. The closest research reviewed in secondary sources concerns related practices such as dry-towel self-massage and general exfoliation.[3]

Khetarpal advises against brushing broken, sunburned, infected, inflamed or irritated skin, moles, warts and raised bumps, and against brushing the face, and she says to stop if skin becomes irritated.[2] News-Medical reports that stiff bristles or long sessions can strip lipids and weaken the moisture barrier, causing stinging, and that people with eczema or acne are generally advised to avoid it. It also advises washing and air-drying brushes to limit microbial growth.[3] Grokipedia lists similar contraindications.[1]

Dry brushing appears in body-care and skin routines as an inexpensive exfoliant. Looksmaxxing forum threads surfaced for this entry mention brushes only incidentally, so no distinct community claims are documented here.
